settings.title: Medical Billing Built Around New Mexico’s Payer Mix

settings.editor:
New Mexico practices submit claims under Medicare, Medicaid and commercial insurance plans, each with its own coverage and billing requirements. Turquoise Care is the state’s Medicaid managed care program that includes four plans: Presbyterian Health Plan, Blue Cross and Blue Shield of New Mexico, UnitedHealthcare Community Plan and Molina Healthcare, each with distinct coverage plans and billing requirements. Only billing operations that run smoothly here know the patient’s specific plan, check for the provider’s network participation, verify authorization and follow claim submission requests.

When expanding this picture, older adults add another dimension to reimbursement source breakdown. More than one in five New Mexico residents are 65 or older. The billing can be even trickier for practices that care for these patients, as it involves Original Medicare, Medicare Advantage, or any additional coverage. For patients covered by both Medicare and Medicaid, identifying the correct payer order, coordinating benefits and checking that documentation supports the billed services are particularly important.

title.value: Medical Billing and Coding in New Mexico: State-Specific Rules

paragraph.value: Your practice needs to track more than claim submission dates. New Mexico’s billing requirements also affect payment follow-up, claim corrections and patient charges.

Under 8.302.2.11 NMAC, applicable Medicaid claims must reach the state or its claims processor within 90 calendar days of service. For inpatient care, the timeline starts at discharge. Newly enrolled providers have 90 days from their approval notice. If eligibility is granted retroactively, the window starts when that eligibility is added.

title.value: One Grace Period for Claim Corrections

paragraph.value: If a timely claim is returned, denied or underpaid, your practice has one 90-day grace period from the remittance date to resubmit or request an adjustment. There is no second grace period. We review the response and address the identified issue before resubmission.

When another payer processes a claim first, your team needs to track its decision date. Under the applicable Medicaid rule, submission is due within 90 days of that decision and no later than 210 days after service. Submitting the primary claim promptly helps leave time for follow-up.

Under 13.10.28.9 NMAC, applicable health carriers must pay clean electronic claims within 30 days and paper claims within 45 days. If payment is late, interest is due within 30 days after the claim is paid. Our team tracks payment dates and follows up on interest that remains unpaid.

title.value: Surprise Billing Payments and Patient Responsibility

paragraph.value: For services covered by New Mexico’s Surprise Billing Protection Act, carriers pay out-of-network providers directly using the applicable state benchmark. FAIR Health describes this as the 60th percentile of allowed commercial rates for the area. Self-funded employer plans generally follow federal protections. Before billing your patients, we check which protections apply and whether their charges are limited to in-network cost-sharing.

title.value: Billing for Native American Patients, IHS, and 638 Facilities

paragraph.value: Your practice may see Native American patients with different Medicaid arrangements. These members generally choose whether to join Turquoise Care, although enrollment is required for long-term care. Your team needs to confirm whether each patient has fee-for-service coverage or an MCO plan. Members can also receive care through Indian Health Service, Tribal 638 and urban Indian programs, even without a contract between the program and their plan (HCA).
We check the patient’s coverage at each visit to identify the applicable billing requirements and help prevent avoidable claim routing errors before submission.

settings.title: Medicaid Fee Schedules and Payment Reviews

settings.editor: When practitioners receive lower payments than expected, they need to know why. Our billing experts compare the payment with the applicable NM Medicaid fee schedule or payer contract. We check the service date and billing conditions to determine whether the difference is valid or needs follow-up. If we identify underpayment, our billing team contacts the payer with supporting documentation to request correction.

There is an applicable deadline NM Medicaid expects practices to submit their claims. That timeline varies, depending on the coverage, payer and circumstances. We track these dates and retain submission records and payer acknowledgement. But if it contains any sort of mistakes, our team follows the payer’s correction and resubmission. Or if a denial needs to be challenged, we follow the appeal procedure within the timeframe.

It is for sure that the care listed on a claim should match the insurance company’s authorization. If the payer approves six therapy sessions within a specific period, the billing team should ensure the claim aligns with the approval. In case of misalignment in the date, services, or units, or if there’s missing information, we alert your practice so the issue can be resolved before submission.

An unpaid insurance balance does not automatically become the patient’s responsibility. The New Mexico Surprise Billing Law and the Federal No Surprises Act limit patient charges in applicable situations. We check whether or not it applies to the patient’s plan beforehand. Our team sends the patient a bill with relevant cost-sharing and balance-billing restrictions to prevent inappropriate charges.

title.value: New Mexico Gross Receipts Tax and Your Billing Records

paragraph.value: New Mexico’s gross receipts tax can apply to your practice’s revenue, although certain healthcare payments qualify for deductions. Keeping those payments recorded helps your tax adviser review which receipts meet the requirements.

settings.title_text: Which Payments May Qualify for a Deduction
settings.description_text: Under Section 7-9-93 NMSA, eligible practitioners can deduct qualifying commercial contract and Medicare Part C payments from managed care organizations and health insurers. Since July 1, 2023, related patient copays and deductibles may also qualify. Fee-for-service payments from indemnity plans do not qualify under this deduction. Hospitals, hospices, nursing homes and outpatient facilities are excluded from its practitioner definition. The deduction requires the designated rate code when filing through the state’s TAP system.

settings.title_text: Payment Posting That Supports Your Tax Review
settings.description_text: When payments are recorded without payer details, separating eligible receipts can take additional work. Our team records the payer and plan type to help distinguish commercial contract payments, Medicare Part C receipts and related patient payments. Your tax adviser determines eligibility and what to claim, using those billing records for support.
